clue.text: One of those golden ones familiar to traveller Keats? ()

definitions.text: One of those golden ones familiar to traveller Keats?

parts.words: One of those golden ones familiar to traveller Keats?
parts.note: Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer opens 'Much have I travell'd in the ... of gold', so the solver wants one of those golden kingdoms

explanation.surface: A question about the golden places a well-travelled Keats knew.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingdom or domain is the kind of place Keats's poem says he wandered through, in golden form.

clue.text: Contribution by late-order batsman recorded by Updike?

explanation.surface: A tail-end cricketer's score, as written up by John Updike.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a 'rabbit' is a hopeless batsman who comes in near the end of the order, so a single he scores is a rabbit's run; Updike's novel shares the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbit is cricket slang for a poor lower-order batsman, and one run he makes is his contribution; John Updike's 1960 novel bears the same title.

clue.text: Burns from hot ashes? On the contrary… ()

definitions.text: Burns from hot ashes? On the contrary…

parts.words: Burns from hot ashes? On the contrary…
parts.note: turned round, the clue asks for hot ashes from Burns: the Scots word Robert Burns used for a glowing ember

explanation.surface: Someone scorched by hot cinders, or perhaps the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' looks like a verb for being scorched; it is the poet Robert Burns, and 'On the contrary' says to swap the two halves round.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Scots dialect word for a live coal or hot cinder, found in the poetry of Robert Burns.

clue.text: Essayist is all mixed up, not enigma

indicators.note: something all mixed up has its parts jumbled, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that an essayist's writing is confused, though it is no puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Michel de Montaigne, the sixteenth-century French writer, invented the essay as a literary form.

clue.text: Artist of some force?

explanation.surface: A painter of real power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' reads as artistic strength; here it is a police force, of which a constable is a member.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable was the English landscape painter; a constable is also a police officer, a member of a force.

clue.text: Hugh Walpole's schoolmaster in the White House?

explanation.surface: A teacher from a Walpole school novel imagined as American president.
explanation.walkthrough: In Walpole's 1911 school novel 'Mr Perrin and Mr Traill' Clinton is one of the junior masters; Bill Clinton later became US president.
explanation.definitionFit: A junior master of that surname teaches in Walpole's school novel, and the same surname belongs to the forty-second American president.

clue.text: Cipher book containing spies' report

parts.note: reads like a spy's codebook, but it is the fourth book of the Bible, whose thirteenth chapter has the report of the twelve spies sent into Canaan, and a cipher is a figure

explanation.surface: An espionage codebook holding an agent's intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all espionage; the Old Testament book in which Moses sends spies into Canaan takes its name from the census figures it records.
explanation.definitionFit: Ciphers are figures, and the Old Testament book named after them includes the account of the spies returning from Canaan.

clue.text: Devonian amphibian immortalized by friend of Lawrence

definitions.text: Devonian amphibian immortalized by friend of Lawrence

parts.words: Devonian amphibian immortalized by friend of Lawrence
parts.note: the otter of Henry Williamson's 1927 novel set in Devon; Williamson was a friend of T. E. Lawrence

explanation.surface: A creature from Devon made famous by an acquaintance of Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devonian' suggests the geological period of early amphibians; it means simply from Devon, and the semi-aquatic animal is an otter.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Williamson's otter hero lives on Devon rivers, and an otter lives both in water and on land.

clue.text: Close relationship in which Fugard unfortunately took blond

indicators.note: the taking went badly wrong, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Athol Fugard, the South African playwright, regrettably chose a fair-haired partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Fugard's play of this title is about two brothers, which fits the close relationship.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie of kinship or deep loyalty is a bond so tight it is likened to one sealed in blood.

clue.text: Successful O'Hara character, consumed, it's said, and haunted by emptiness of achievement

indicators.note: the word is spoken rather than written, so a word sounding the same is entered

parts.note: consumed means eaten, as food is

explanation.surface: A thriving John O'Hara hero, eaten up and haunted by the hollowness of his success.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Eaton is the hero of John O'Hara's 'From the Terrace', a businessman who succeeds yet finds it empty; the last words describe him.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Eaton rises to wealth and status in John O'Hara's 1958 novel, so he is the prosperous figure meant.

clue.text: Holy city familiar to traveller Yeats

definitions.text: Holy city familiar to traveller Yeats

parts.words: Holy city familiar to traveller Yeats
parts.note: points to Yeats's poem in which the speaker sails to the holy city of Constantinople under its old name

explanation.surface: A sacred town well known to the voyaging poet Yeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's poem 'Sailing to ...' calls the old capital of the Eastern Roman Empire a holy city.

clue.text: This where curses came to, said Southey ()

definitions.text: This where curses came to, said Southey

parts.words: This where curses came to, said Southey
parts.note: Southey wrote that curses are like young chickens: they always come home to their perch

explanation.surface: Southey remarking on where curses end up.
explanation.definitionFit: A perch where chickens settle for the night is where Southey says curses return.

clue.text: Succoured by Sir Artegal, she reigned in peace in Erin (a mistake?)

definitions.text: Succoured by Sir Artegal, she reigned in peace

indicators.note: followed by a question mark, the suggestion that these letters are an error says they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rescued queen ruling peacefully in Ireland, with a doubt over the spelling.
explanation.walkthrough: In Book V of Spenser's 'The Faerie Queene' Sir Artegall rescues the lady Irena, whose name comes from Greek eirene, peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's Irena is restored to her kingdom by Artegall, and her name means peace in Greek.

clue.text: Where Marvell fell on grass (6)

parts.note: in Andrew Marvell's poem the speaker, ensnared with flowers, falls on grass among melons and fruit trees

explanation.surface: The place where the poet Marvell tumbled onto the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The '(6)' points to the sixth stanza of Marvell's poem, where the line 'Ensnar'd with flowers, I fall on grass' occurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvell's poem of that title is set among the plants and fruit of a cultivated plot.

clue.text: As a physicist, he could see through anybody

definitions.text: As a physicist, he could see through anybody

parts.words: As a physicist, he could see through anybody
parts.note: a perceptive person sees through people figuratively; this physicist discovered X-rays, which see through bodies literally

explanation.surface: A scientist so shrewd no one could fool him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See through anybody' reads as shrewdness; read literally it is the X-ray.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, rays that pass through the human body.

clue.text: "I have but —— in ready money, but I can draw for a thousand pounds" (Addison)

definitions.text: "I have but —— in ready money, but I can draw for a thousand pounds" (Addison)

parts.words: "I have but —— in ready money, but I can draw for a thousand pounds" (Addison)
parts.note: a fill-in: Addison's line contrasts a few small coins in the pocket with credit for a large sum

explanation.surface: A quotation from Joseph Addison about being short of cash but good for credit.
explanation.walkthrough: Addison said this of a conversationalist with little small talk but great reserves of thought; the missing sum is a small pre-decimal British coin amount, nine old pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine old British pennies is a trifling sum of ready cash set against a thousand pounds of credit.

clue.text: Jonsonian protagonist, partly wise (Janus-faced, however)

indicators.note: only part of the following words is taken, so the letters are found running within them

explanation.surface: A character of Ben Jonson's, somewhat wise but two-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's tragedy 'Sejanus His Fall' is about the treacherous favourite of Tiberius, so 'Janus-faced' fits him too.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's Roman tragedy takes its title from its central figure, the scheming minister of Tiberius.

clue.text: Fragrant wood of H. E. Bates

definitions.text: Fragrant wood of H. E. Bates

parts.words: Fragrant wood of H. E. Bates
parts.note: H. E. Bates wrote 'The ... Tree', named after a tropical tree with scented timber

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling timber associated with the novelist H. E. Bates.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical American tree gives a scented hardwood and lends its name to Bates's 1949 novel set in Burma.

clue.text: In abeyance, like Waugh work

explanation.surface: Something put on hold, like one of Evelyn Waugh's books.
explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn Waugh's unfinished novel is 'Work Suspended'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something halted for the time being is held off, and Waugh left his novel 'Work Suspended' unfinished.

clue.text: … from the Of thy chaste breast, and quiet mind" (Lovelace)

definitions.text: … from the Of thy chaste breast, and quiet mind" (Lovelace)

parts.words: … from the Of thy chaste breast, and quiet mind" (Lovelace)
parts.note: a fill-in from Lovelace's 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars': the poet flies to war from the cloister of his lady's chaste breast

explanation.surface: Lines from Richard Lovelace about leaving a beloved's pure heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The full lines are 'That from the ... / Of thy chaste breast, and quiet mind, / To war and arms I fly'; the gap marker has dropped from the clue as held.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovelace compares Lucasta's chaste breast to a convent where holy women live apart from the world.

clue.text: One of James's junior companions?

parts.note: the outlaw Jesse James rode with brothers surnamed for being less old, and junior means less old

explanation.surface: A question about one of James's young friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'James' suggests the novelist Henry James; it is Jesse James, whose gang included the brothers Cole, Jim and Bob of this surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Junior means of fewer years, and the brothers who rode with Jesse James bore that comparative as a surname.

clue.text: Implied American historian

parts.note: something implied is unspoken, or tacit
US is short for American, from United States

explanation.surface: A historian from America who is merely hinted at.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacitus was the Roman historian who wrote the Annals and Histories.

clue.text: Some Dubliners who are passed over

explanation.surface: Some people of Dublin who are ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: The final story of Joyce's 'Dubliners' has this title; 'passed over' here means having died.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's collection ends with this story, and those who have passed over have died.

clue.text: That of Henry Green's fog-bound travellers was symbolically delayed

definitions.text: That of Henry Green's fog-bound travellers was symbolically delayed

parts.words: That of Henry Green's fog-bound travellers was symbolically delayed
parts.note: in Henry Green's 'Party Going' a party of rich young people is stuck at a London station by fog, unable to set off

explanation.surface: Henry Green's travellers, caught by fog, had their trip put back with symbolic weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting off on a journey is what Green's stranded travellers cannot do while the fog holds their train.

clue.text: The purport of James Hanley

explanation.surface: The meaning of the novelist James Hanley's work.
explanation.walkthrough: James Hanley's first novel, published in 1930, has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The gist or general meaning of something is its tenor, and Hanley's 1930 novel has the same title.

clue.text: The red ones were for Sean O'Casey

definitions.text: The red ones were for Sean O'Casey

parts.words: The red ones were for Sean O'Casey
parts.note: O'Casey's play 'Red ... for Me' names the flowers in its title

explanation.surface: Red things set aside for the playwright Sean O'Casey.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Casey's 1943 play takes its title from red flowers given to a lover.

clue.text: Point in trick ballet

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, as in says

parts.note: a trick is a ruse
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: The key moment in a deceptive dance performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word meaning Russian appears in 'ballet russe', the Russian ballet company style.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for Russian, as in Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, stands for that company's kind of dance.

clue.text: Weighty novelist Entries submitted from

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Weighty novelist Entries submitted from (5)': 'Entries submitted from' is page boilerplate run into the clue, so the printed clue is garbled and no scan is available.

clue.text: Point in pub's novelist ()

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, as in says

parts.note: a pub is an inn; the possessive reads as plural
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A novelist's key point made in a public house.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Innes was the pen name of J. I. M. Stewart, writer of donnish detective novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Innes wrote the Inspector Appleby detective stories.

clue.text: Hardy tree

parts.note: a tree that is hardy survives cold, but here it is Thomas Hardy's novel 'Under the ... Tree'

explanation.surface: A tough tree that survives the winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective; it is Thomas Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's novel 'Under the ... Tree' is named after a woodland, and the word describes leafy forest.

clue.text: Highly valued, like Palgrave's anthology?

explanation.surface: Prized, as Palgrave's collection of verse was.
explanation.walkthrough: Palgrave's famous anthology is 'The Golden Treasury', so something put in it might be said to be treasure-d.
explanation.definitionFit: Something highly valued is cherished, and Palgrave's Golden Treasury is a store of prized poems.

clue.text: Correct end of prayer with daughter

parts.note: amen is said at the close of a prayer
D is the abbreviation for daughter in genealogies

explanation.surface: Getting the end of a prayer right with one's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: To correct something is to revise it, making it right.
